post:2026-10-09.text:
A product can look finished while its most important decision is still unresolved.

The homepage says who it is for. The onboarding asks for information. The dashboard presents a set of actions. Somewhere between those screens, the user has to understand what to do next and why it is worth doing.

That is the part of design I want to talk about more here.

My background spans product design, creative direction, brand strategy, and startup founding. I’m interested in how those disciplines inform the decisions an early team makes.

For a product review, I would start with one task: follow a new user from the first promise to the first useful outcome. Write down every point where the next step needs an explanation. Then ask which of those explanations belongs in the experience itself.

It is a practical starting point for a conversation between a founder and a designer. It gives us something specific to examine before deciding what to redesign.

Where does a new user need the most help understanding your product today?

post:2026-10-13.text:
If your brand says "simple", try creating an account in your own product.

Notice the things a new customer has to work out. Why do you need this information? What happens after clicking continue? Can they change that choice later?

Each unanswered question adds a bit of work. A shorter form won't help much if people still don't understand what they're signing up for.

I'd take one word from the brand strategy and review the product against it. For "trusted", that might mean showing the price before asking for payment details. For "clear", it might mean saying exactly what a button will do.

My work spans brand strategy and product design. This is where I like to connect them: a promise someone can actually see in the product.

Which part of your first-use experience needs a better explanation?

Counting onboarding screens won't tell you whether someone is ready to use the product.

I'd check what a new customer can do after each step. After entering company details, can they create the thing they signed up to make? After inviting a teammate, do they know what that person can access?

post:2026-10-11:1800.text:
A founder and a designer can hear the same customer call and come away with different problems to solve.

The founder might hear a request for a missing feature. The designer might notice that the customer couldn't find something already in the product.

I'd want both of those observations in the discussion before anyone commits to a solution. Ask the customer to walk through what they were trying to do. Watch where they get stuck. Then compare that with what each person thought the problem was.

The designer can lead the session while the founder listens and asks follow-ups. Afterwards, agree on what you actually heard and which questions still need testing.

At an early startup, those conversations belong in the same room as product decisions.

Translating a brand promise into your product means more than just words on a page. It shapes how the interface behaves, the language it uses, and even how support interacts with customers. For example, if your brand promises simplicity, your interface should avoid clutter and guide users clearly through tasks. The language should be straightforward, avoiding jargon, and support should respond with patience and clarity.

For founders, a practical step is to review the product experience through the lens of your brand promise. Ask: Does every interaction reflect what we say we stand for? This can be as simple as running a brand-review prompt during product sprints, checking if the UI, messaging, and support align. That review helps catch disconnects early, so your product feels consistent and trustworthy from the first touch.

posts.text:
A product can look finished while its most important decision is still unresolved.

The homepage says who it is for. The onboarding asks for information. The dashboard presents a set of actions. Somewhere between those screens, the user has to understand what to do next and why it is worth doing.

That is the part of design I want to talk about more here.

My background spans product design, creative direction, brand strategy, and startup founding. I’m interested in how those disciplines inform the decisions an early team makes.

For a product review, I would start with one task: follow a new user from the first promise to the first useful outcome. Write down every point where the next step needs an explanation. Then ask which of those explanations belongs in the experience itself.

It is a practical starting point for a conversation between a founder and a designer. It gives us something specific to examine before deciding what to redesign.

Where does a new user need the most help understanding your product today?

If your brand says "simple", try creating an account in your own product.

Notice the things a new customer has to work out. Why do you need this information? What happens after clicking continue? Can they change that choice later?

Each unanswered question adds a bit of work. A shorter form won't help much if people still don't understand what they're signing up for.

I'd take one word from the brand strategy and review the product against it. For "trusted", that might mean showing the price before asking for payment details. For "clear", it might mean saying exactly what a button will do.

My work spans brand strategy and product design. This is where I like to connect them: a promise someone can actually see in the product.

Which part of your first-use experience needs a better explanation?

I'm looking for founding designer opportunities and building a consulting practice around product design and brand strategy.

I've worked across creative direction, product design, startup founding, and brand strategy. I want to bring that mix to early teams while there's still room to question the brief.

The first conversation I'd want to have is about the customer. What are they trying to do? Where are they getting stuck? What does the team already know, and what are we guessing?

A rough prototype can give that conversation something concrete. Walk through it together and notice where you disagree. Those moments can tell you what to test next.

If you're looking for a founding designer or considering outside design help, tell me which product decision your team is wrestling with. We can start there.

Before opening Figma, write down what someone came to this screen to do.

Say it's an invoice dashboard. A customer opens it because they need to find an unpaid invoice and send a reminder. Can they spot that invoice, understand its status, and send it without hunting through menus?

That's a useful design review. "Make the dashboard cleaner" gives everyone a different problem to solve.

I'd follow the task through the screen once and note each moment that needs explaining. Maybe the status label is vague. Maybe the reminder action is buried. Fix those before spending another afternoon on the card layout.

The visual details still matter. Choosing them gets easier when the team agrees on the task the screen needs to help with.

If you're hiring your first designer, let them into the conversation before the feature list is settled.

Give them the customer calls. Show them the support questions. Explain which assumptions are keeping you up at night.

A designer can turn an uncertain idea into a flow that the team can walk through. Sometimes that exposes a missing step. Sometimes it reveals that two features are trying to solve the same problem.

If the brief only arrives after those decisions, you've already limited what the designer can help with.

I'm interested in founding designer roles where that conversation happens early. My background spans product design, creative direction, brand strategy, and startup founding. I'd want to understand what your customers are struggling with before deciding what to draw.

Counting onboarding screens won't tell you whether someone is ready to use the product.

I'd check what a new customer can do after each step. After entering company details, can they create the thing they signed up to make? After inviting a teammate, do they know what that person can access?

A short setup flow can still leave people confused. A longer one may be useful if every step helps them finish a task.

For the next review, I'd follow one customer goal through setup and write down where progress stops. Maybe the question needs an example. Maybe the next action is unclear. That gives the team a specific change to test.

A founder and a designer can hear the same customer call and come away with different problems to solve.

The founder might hear a request for a missing feature. The designer might notice that the customer couldn't find something already in the product.

I'd want both of those observations in the discussion before anyone commits to a solution. Ask the customer to walk through what they were trying to do. Watch where they get stuck. Then compare that with what each person thought the problem was.

The designer can lead the session while the founder listens and asks follow-ups. Afterwards, agree on what you actually heard and which questions still need testing.

At an early startup, those conversations belong in the same room as product decisions.

Translating a brand promise into your product means more than just words on a page. It shapes how the interface behaves, the language it uses, and even how support interacts with customers. For example, if your brand promises simplicity, your interface should avoid clutter and guide users clearly through tasks. The language should be straightforward, avoiding jargon, and support should respond with patience and clarity.

For founders, a practical step is to review the product experience through the lens of your brand promise. Ask: Does every interaction reflect what we say we stand for? This can be as simple as running a brand-review prompt during product sprints, checking if the UI, messaging, and support align. That review helps catch disconnects early, so your product feels consistent and trustworthy from the first touch.

A product can look familiar and still have a clear point of view. The choice often sits in what gets the most attention, what takes fewer steps and what you leave out.

For a scheduling tool, that might mean making the next available time easy to find before showing the full calendar. For a finance tool, it might mean explaining a balance before offering another chart. These are hypothetical choices, each tied to a different customer task.

I'd use the four questions on this card before discussing visual references. They give the team something concrete to agree on.

A claim such as 'a report in minutes' creates a product requirement. The team then has to decide what counts as a report, when the clock starts and which prerequisites the customer should know about.

This carousel follows a hypothetical reporting tool from the website to its first result. An undisclosed approval step is the point where the claim and the experience separate. There are several possible responses, including a narrower promise or a sample the customer can try immediately.

If a product decision is holding your early-stage team back, describe the problem in the comments. I am building my consulting practice and would welcome a relevant conversation.

A redesign request often combines a customer getting stuck, an unresolved product rule and a preference about the visual direction. I want those recorded separately before the team approves a larger piece of work.

This worksheet uses a hypothetical pricing-page example. It shows how to record an observation, keep the explanation open, compare a local fix with a wider redesign and choose a test that could change the decision.

The downloadable version has room for your own evidence and includes a review rubric. Use it in the approval meeting. If the observation is missing, the next useful piece of work is to find out what happens during the task.

Download the worksheet: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/designwithrupesh/linkedingrowthengine/main/resources/linkedin/redesign-evidence-worksheet.pdf

Sharing unfinished work can feel riskier than sending a finished presentation. The person wants help, but they may still be changing their mind.

For a hypothetical review tool, I'd let the creator send a separate copy for comments while keeping the working draft private. The invitation would name the reviewer, show their access and identify the version they will see.

That choice has a cost. A frozen review copy won't include later edits automatically. The product needs to explain that limit and make updates deliberate.

I'd want a founding designer in this discussion before Share becomes a button on a finished screen. The decision shapes permissions, versioning and how comfortable someone feels asking for feedback.

A design critique gets more useful when someone describes what the customer is trying to do and how the screen might make that moment feel.

Take a hypothetical checkout. A customer is checking the delivery address before paying. A large urgent button, a hidden total and an ambiguous back link create a very different conversation from a clear order summary with an obvious way to correct a mistake.

I'd ask the team to walk through that decision before collecting visual references. Which information helps someone feel ready to continue? What can they still change? Where does the product need to slow down?

Those answers give the visual direction a job. They also give the team something more useful to discuss than whether a layout feels premium.

If your product experience and brand promise feel disconnected, I would welcome a conversation about the decision your team is working through.

A Share button can carry several different intentions. Someone might want a quick comment, a formal review or a public release. Treating those as the same action leaves a lot for them to guess.

This hypothetical review tool follows a creator who needs feedback while the draft is still changing. The proposed flow sends a separate copy to named reviewers. The working draft stays private.

The cost is version drift. A reviewer may be discussing an older copy, so the product needs to keep that boundary visible and let the creator choose when to update it.

That's the kind of product question I want to work through with early teams: what the action means to a person, which rules support it and how the interface makes those rules clear.

I'm open to founding designer conversations with early-stage teams.

My background spans 11 years across creative direction, product design, startup founding and brand strategy. I want to bring that range to a team while the product's basic decisions are still open.

I'd want to understand the customer problem, what the business needs to prove and the experience people should have when they use the product. From there, the work might be a rough flow, a visual direction or a prototype that helps the team settle a disagreement.

I care about how those pieces hold together. The product's language, behavior and appearance all give people reasons to trust it, or reasons to hesitate.

If your early-stage team is shaping its product and design foundations, I would welcome a conversation about the role.

Before adding a Share button, I'd ask the team to draw what crosses the boundary.

Is it the live document or a frozen copy? Does the other person get permission to view, comment or edit? If the owner closes access, what can they actually take back?

Use the two-page map for that conversation. The first page works through a hypothetical review tool. The second gives your team room to map its own states and write one clear rule before the next mockup.

The awkward questions matter here. Closing access can stop future viewing; it cannot recall a screenshot. A quiet interface still needs an honest explanation of that limit.

I'm open to consulting conversations with founders working through product decisions like this.

Download the worksheet: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/designwithrupesh/linkedingrowthengine/main/resources/linkedin/stories/sharing-state-map.pdf

An empty search result can make someone wonder whether the product has lost their work.

Imagine a project library with no matches after a filter is applied. The person may have spent hours on those files. A bare No results message leaves them to work out whether the files are gone, the search failed or the filter is too narrow.

I'd keep the active filters visible, explain what was searched and offer a direct way back to all projects. If the search itself failed, the screen should say that clearly.

The visual treatment needs to support the same explanation. An illustration of an empty box might suggest there is no work at all, which would be the wrong story in this example.

I want the person to understand what happened and feel able to recover. What does your product say when someone's work seems to disappear?

An empty state asks the customer to do work before the product has shown much of its value. The copy needs to make that effort understandable.

In this hypothetical invoicing screen, 'Get started' leaves several questions open. What am I creating? What will I need? Will it be sent immediately? The revised screen answers those questions before the click and explains what the view will show afterward.

I'd test this without an introduction from the team. If the person can explain the next action and what it will do, the empty state is doing its job.

Country is a rough guess at language.

Framer's October 1 Firewall update can redirect or block visitors by country and URL path. That's useful control for a site with regional pages.

But a visitor in the Netherlands might still want the English version. Someone travelling may want the version they use at home.

I'm comfortable using location to suggest a locale. Automatically choosing it needs an obvious way back and a way to remember the person's choice. That's the part of the experience I'd check before turning a rule on.

Release notes: https://www.framer.com/updates/firewall

Notion has put a permission control inside the database column menu. I like that placement.

In the October 13 release, property access lets an owner decide which columns a person or agent can view or edit. The screenshot labels it Alpha.

Putting it beside Edit property makes sense. You're already thinking about that column.

What I can't judge from this image is the other side: what does someone with restricted access see? A missing field can look like missing data. That experience needs just as much care as the owner's menu.

Official Notion release image: https://www.notion.com/releases/2026-10-13

I like a quiet interface. I get suspicious when 'cleaner' is the whole argument for a redesign.

Sometimes the screen looks cleaner because useful controls have been moved into a menu. The screenshot improves; the person doing the same task now has another place to look.

Show me the before and after while someone is trying to finish something. That's a much more interesting design conversation.

Linear's October 8 update puts a pull request in the context of its stack. In this screenshot, the current change is number 3, with the surrounding changes still visible.

The numbering, connecting line and Current label make the position clear without much explanation. I like that.

The faded neighbouring rows are my hesitation. On a smaller screen, context that's technically there may still be hard to read. I'd want to see this at review size before calling the hierarchy a win.

Official Linear release image: https://linear.app/changelog/2026-10-08-stacked-pull-requests

I'm starting consulting conversations around product design and brand strategy.

The work I'm interested in often sits between the two. A product promises simplicity, but its first task needs an explanation. Or the landing page speaks to one customer while the interface seems designed for someone else.

I'd want to understand that mismatch before proposing a new visual direction.

If your team is circling a decision like this, tell me what you're trying to settle.

Penpot calling Auto layout 'Flex layout' is a useful difference to talk about when a team changes tools.

Its October 15 Figma terminology guide explains the naming. The Inspect image shows a selected Flex layout and display: flex in the CSS panel beside it.

That connection interests me more than learning that Frames are called Boards. It gives designers and developers something concrete to point at when they discuss layout behaviour.

A terminology guide is a starting point. Before moving a team, I'd still rebuild a familiar component and see which habits carry over.

Official Penpot guide and image: https://penpot.app/blog/figma-to-penpot-terminology-cheatsheet/

If you're showing me a redesign, show me the mistake too.

Open something without permission, or delete the wrong item and try to get it back.

I want to see how the product talks to someone at that moment. A calm hero screen tells me very little about that part of the experience.

The recovery screens deserve a place in the presentation.

UX, UI, visual design, research, interaction design. A glossary is handy when a job description uses all of them to mean 'the designer'.

Nielsen Norman Group has published definitions for these disciplines. I'd use it at the start of a hiring conversation: which responsibilities does the team actually need, and which ones will this hire have the time and support to cover?

I can work across creative direction, product design and brand strategy. I still want the brief to be clear. Breadth shouldn't turn into an undefined job.

https://www.nngroup.com/articles/ux-disciplines-glossary/

Equal-looking columns can still have different layout rules.

Penpot's 1fr tracks make the choice explicit here. I want that intent in the file, so a later change doesn't start with guessing which widths were meant to stay together.

Official Penpot screenshot:
https://penpot.app/blog/declarative-design-with-penpot/

Bring the screen that keeps coming back into review.

A redesign brief is stronger when it points to one unresolved moment. 'Make it cleaner' can wait until the team agrees what needs to change.

The attached intake sheet is fillable. If your team is stuck on a redesign, I'm open to a consulting conversation.

Download the worksheet: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/designwithrupesh/linkedingrowthengine/main/resources/linkedin/oct26/redesign-intake-sheet.pdf

DHL gives the parent page an 'Overview' link inside the expanded branch.

That's the arrangement I prefer. The row can open the menu without also trying to take me to a page. The two actions get two clear places.

DHL screenshot via Smashing Magazine:
https://www.smashingmagazine.com/2026/10/accordion-icons-which-work-best/

A Slack reply can confirm a setup and still leave the saved rule hard to find.

Linear's demo says what will trigger the loop and where it will post. The last page is my proposal for the record behind that reply: who owns it, what starts it and where to pause it.

The demo frames and the proposed screen are labelled separately.
https://linear.app/changelog/2026-10-22-slack-and-github-loops

Keep the type decisions attached to the label.

In Penpot's Inspect view, 'Services' sits beside its font, weight and line-height. The next person can read the values behind this bit of the interface instead of measuring a picture.

Official Penpot screenshot:
https://penpot.app/blog/declarative-design-with-penpot/

When opening the address is the main task, the row should do one thing.

The pencil creates a second destination in what looks like the same control. Put 'Edit address' inside the details, or make editing the main action from the start.

An illustrative interaction study, informed by:
https://www.smashingmagazine.com/2026/10/accordion-icons-which-work-best/

Give the first designer a boundary they can work inside.

A checkout review can have an owner, a checkpoint and an explicit list of work that will wait. 'Own design' leaves all of that open.

The attached scope sheet is fillable. Use it with the founder and engineering lead before turning the role into a list of deliverables.

Download the worksheet: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/designwithrupesh/linkedingrowthengine/main/resources/linkedin/oct26/first-design-hire-scope.pdf

An automation setup should leave something you can come back to.

Linear's Slack reply says it will post customer follow-ups here after each relevant merge. I like having that promise in the same place as the request.

Official Linear demo:
https://linear.app/changelog/2026-10-22-slack-and-github-loops

The fact that AI saves time on nearly every task but practitioners remain lukewarm is a key design insight. It shows that automation doesn’t just speed up work; it changes the trust in design decisions. When AI generates outputs that aren’t reliable or require constant oversight, it creates a recovery path problem: designers lose confidence in their own judgment. That’s not a flaw in the tool, but in how we design the feedback loop between AI and human judgment. The real design challenge isn’t adoption, it’s maintaining trust through transparency and control.

Source: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/ai-in-ux-survey-26/
